q: Annual credit purchases of an enterprise are Rs 7,20,000 and its average creditors are Rs 1,20,000. Taking a year of 360 days, the average payment period is:

options.D: 50 days

e: Average payment period = Average creditors / Annual credit purchases x 360 = 1,20,000 / 7,20,000 x 360 = 60 days.

q: A supplier offers credit terms of 3/10, net 45. The approximate annual cost of not taking the cash discount (on a 360-day year basis) is:
e: Cost of not taking the discount = [3 / (100 - 3)] x [360 / (45 - 10)] = 3.09% x 10.29, which is approximately 31.8% per annum, making this source of credit very costly.

q: Under a factoring arrangement for receivables:

options.A: The bank lends money against the security of fixed assets
options.B: The debtors are asked to pay for the goods in advance
options.C: The receivables are insured against changes in market prices
options.D: The receivables are sold/assigned to a factor, who collects the dues from the customers and may also bear the risk of bad debts, for a fee or commission

e: In factoring, the receivables are sold or assigned to a factor, who collects the dues from customers and, under a non-recourse arrangement, may also bear the bad-debt risk, all for a fee or commission.

q: In appraising the credit-worthiness of a customer, the 'Five Cs of credit' refer to:

options.A: Character, Capacity, Capital, Collateral and Conditions
options.B: Cash, Credit, Cost, Control and Collection
options.C: Customer, Commodity, Credit period, Collection and Commission
options.D: Capital, Current assets, Creditors, Cash flow and Costs

e: The Five Cs of credit appraisal are Character, Capacity, Capital, Collateral and Conditions - the standard heads under which a customer's credit-worthiness is judged before granting credit.

q: An 'aging schedule' of receivables is a statement which:

options.A: Shows the date of manufacture of each product sold
options.B: Classifies the outstanding debtors according to the length of time for which they have been outstanding, so that slow-paying accounts can be identified and followed up
options.C: Fixes the retirement age of the credit sales staff
options.D: Lists the depreciation charged on old assets

e: An aging schedule classifies the outstanding debtors according to the length of time for which each amount has been outstanding, so that slow-paying accounts can be identified and followed up.

q: Under the Baumol model of cash management, an enterprise's annual cash requirement is Rs 15,00,000, the cost of converting marketable securities into cash is Rs 30 per transaction and the opportunity interest rate is 10% per annum. The optimum cash balance, sqrt(2AT/i), is:
e: Optimum cash balance = sqrt(2 x 15,00,000 x 30 / 0.10) = sqrt(90,00,00,000) = Rs 30,000, the balance at which total conversion and opportunity costs are minimised.

q: Under the Miller-Orr model of cash management, an enterprise fixes a lower control limit of Rs 20,000 and a spread of Rs 60,000 between the control limits. The return point (target cash balance) is:
e: Return point = Lower limit + one-third of the spread = 20,000 + (60,000 / 3) = Rs 40,000; cash returning to this point triggers purchase or sale of securities under the Miller-Orr model.

q: 'Concentration banking' as a technique of cash management means:

options.A: Depositing collections in local banks at the various collection centres and transferring the funds promptly to a central (concentration) account, so as to reduce collection float and put the funds to use quickly
options.B: Keeping all the cash of the enterprise in a single office safe
options.C: Borrowing the maximum amount from one bank only
options.D: Paying all the creditors from one branch so that payments are delayed

e: Under concentration banking, collections are deposited in local banks at the various collection centres and transferred promptly to a central concentration account, reducing collection float and putting funds to use quickly.

q: A cash budget differs from a cash flow statement prepared under AS-3 in that the cash budget:

options.A: Is prepared by the statutory auditor of the enterprise
options.B: Is a forecast of the expected cash receipts and payments for a future period, whereas the cash flow statement reports the actual cash flows of a past period
options.D: Is prepared only by government companies

e: A cash budget is a forecast of expected cash receipts and payments for a future period, whereas the cash flow statement under AS-3 reports the actual cash flows of a past period.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 4,50,000 on capital employed of Rs 30,00,000. The Return on Investment of the division is:
e: Return on Investment = Profit / Capital employed x 100 = 4,50,000 / 30,00,000 x 100 = 15%.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 5,00,000 on capital employed of Rs 40,00,000. The cost of capital is 10%. The Residual Income of the division is:
e: Residual Income = Profit - (Cost of capital x Capital employed) = 5,00,000 - (10% x 40,00,000) = 5,00,000 - 4,00,000 = Rs 1,00,000.

q: Economic Value Added (EVA) is computed as:

options.A: Net profit after tax plus depreciation
options.D: Net Operating Profit After Tax (NOPAT) minus a capital charge equal to the capital employed multiplied by the cost of capital

e: EVA = Net Operating Profit After Tax minus a capital charge, the capital charge being capital employed multiplied by the cost of capital; a positive EVA shows value created over and above the cost of capital.

q: A 'discretionary cost centre' (such as a research or legal department) is a responsibility centre in which:

options.A: The output can be measured precisely in monetary terms
options.B: The output cannot be measured in financial terms and there is no clearly defined relationship between inputs and outputs, so performance is judged mainly by adherence to the budget
options.D: The manager has full discretion to fix the selling prices

e: In a discretionary cost centre the output cannot be measured in financial terms and the input-output relationship is not clearly defined, so performance is judged mainly by adherence to the budget.

q: The 'segment margin' of a division, used in judging its profitability, is computed as:

options.C: The segment's contribution minus its traceable (direct) fixed costs, the common fixed costs not being deducted
options.D: The net profit after tax of the whole company apportioned to the segment

e: Segment margin = Segment contribution minus the segment's traceable (direct) fixed costs; common fixed costs are not deducted because they are not incurred for that segment specifically.

q: In the Balanced Scorecard framework, a 'strategy map' serves to:

options.A: Depict the cause-and-effect links by which improvements in learning and growth lead to better internal processes, better customer outcomes and ultimately better financial results
options.B: Show the geographical locations of the branches of the organisation
options.C: Record the scores of employees in their annual appraisals
options.D: Map the authority structure of the organisation

e: A strategy map depicts the cause-and-effect links of the Balanced Scorecard: improvements in learning and growth lead to better internal processes, then better customer outcomes and ultimately better financial results.

q: Which of the following measures belongs to the 'customer' perspective of the Balanced Scorecard?

options.D: Customer retention rate and market share

e: Customer retention rate and market share measure performance from the customer perspective; return on capital employed is financial, training hours relate to learning and growth, and defective units to internal processes.

q: Management audit in India is:

options.A: Compulsory for all companies under the Companies Act
options.B: Not statutorily compulsory; it is a voluntary, systematic appraisal of the efficiency of management, usually carried out at the instance of the management itself
options.C: Conducted only by the Comptroller and Auditor General
options.D: The same as the statutory audit of accounts

e: Management audit is not statutorily compulsory; it is a voluntary, systematic appraisal of the efficiency of management, usually carried out at the instance of the management itself, unlike the statutory audit of accounts.

q: In value engineering, the 'value' of a product or component is best expressed as:

options.A: Its selling price divided by its weight
options.B: Its cost divided by its selling price
options.C: The function it performs divided by its cost — value improves when the essential function is achieved at a lower cost
options.D: Its cost plus a normal margin of profit

e: In value engineering, value = Function / Cost; value is improved when the essential function is achieved reliably at a lower cost, without impairing quality or performance.

q: A product gives a throughput of Rs 500 per unit and takes 0.5 hour of the bottleneck machine per unit. The return per factory hour is:

options.D: Rs 750

e: Return per factory hour = Throughput per unit / Bottleneck hours per unit = 500 / 0.5 = Rs 1,000 per factory hour.

q: Under the Current Cost Accounting (CCA) method of inflation accounting:

options.A: Historical cost accounts are restated with the help of a general price index
options.B: Only the monetary items are adjusted for price changes
options.C: Assets are valued at their current replacement cost (value to the business), with adjustments for depreciation, cost of sales and monetary working capital
options.D: Inflation is ignored and historical costs are retained

e: Under Current Cost Accounting, assets are valued at their current replacement cost (value to the business), with adjustments for depreciation, cost of sales and monetary working capital; a general price index is used under the CPP method instead.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes product costs from period costs?

options.A: Product costs are charged against the revenue of the period in which they are incurred, while period costs are carried forward in inventory
options.B: Product costs (manufacturing costs) are included in the value of inventory and charged when the goods are sold, while period costs such as selling and administration expenses are charged against the revenue of the period in which they are incurred
options.C: Product costs are always fixed in nature, while period costs are always variable
options.D: There is no difference between the two; the terms are used interchangeably

e: Product costs (manufacturing costs) are included in inventory valuation and charged against revenue when the goods are sold, while period costs such as selling and administration expenses are charged in the period incurred.

q: A 'step cost' is a cost which:

options.A: Varies in direct proportion to the level of activity at all levels
options.B: Remains constant in total at every level of activity, however high the output
options.C: Remains constant in total over a range of activity but increases by a discrete step when a threshold level is crossed, e.g., the salary of an additional supervisor when a second shift is started
options.D: Increases continuously with the passage of time, like rent under an escalation clause

e: A step cost remains constant in total over a range of activity but increases by a discrete step when a threshold is crossed, for example the salary of an additional supervisor when a second shift is started.

q: A 'controllable cost' is best defined as:

options.A: A cost which can be influenced by the action of the manager of a responsibility centre within a given period of time
options.B: Any variable cost incurred by a department
options.C: Any cost that is directly traceable to a product
options.D: A cost whose amount is fixed by the top management for the whole enterprise

e: A controllable cost is one that can be influenced by the action of the manager of a responsibility centre within a given period of time; controllability is judged at that manager's level.

q: The total cost of producing 6,000 units is Rs 45,000 and that of producing 10,000 units is Rs 65,000. Using the high-low method, the fixed cost is:
e: By the high-low method, variable cost per unit = (65,000 - 45,000) / (10,000 - 6,000) = Rs 5. Fixed cost = 45,000 - (6,000 x 5) = Rs 15,000.

q: Batch costing is:

options.A: Another name for process costing, applied to continuous production
options.B: A variant of job costing in which a batch of similar articles is treated as the cost unit and the cost is ascertained for the batch as a whole
options.C: A method in which every single article is costed separately, exactly like a job
options.D: A method used only for costing the services of a transport undertaking

e: Batch costing is a variant of job costing in which a batch of similar articles is treated as the cost unit and the cost is ascertained for the batch as a whole.

q: Under a periodic inventory system:

options.A: Inventory is determined by physical counting at the end of the accounting period and the cost of goods sold is derived as a balancing figure, no continuous stock records being maintained
options.B: A continuous record of receipts, issues and balances of every item is maintained throughout the year
options.C: Stock verification is carried out daily for every item in the stores
options.D: The balance of every item of stock is known at any moment from the stores ledger

e: Under a periodic inventory system, inventory is found by physical counting at the end of the accounting period and the cost of goods sold is derived as a balancing figure; no continuous stock records are kept.

q: Under the two-bin system of inventory control:

options.A: Every item of material is stored in two separate stores buildings
options.B: Two bin cards are maintained for each item, one by the storekeeper and one by the accounts office
options.C: Items of stock are classified into two categories only, fast-moving and slow-moving
options.D: Stock is kept in two bins; when the first bin is emptied, it signals that a fresh order must be placed, and consumption continues from the second (reserve) bin during the lead time

e: Under the two-bin system, stock is kept in two bins; when the first bin is emptied it signals that a fresh order must be placed, and consumption continues from the second (reserve) bin during the lead time.

q: The maximum consumption of a material is 250 units per week and the maximum delivery period is 6 weeks. The re-order level for the material is:

options.D: 1,250 units

e: Re-order level = Maximum consumption x Maximum delivery period = 250 x 6 = 1,500 units.

q: The re-order level of a material is 2,600 units and the re-order quantity is 1,800 units. Minimum consumption is 200 units per week and the minimum delivery period is 3 weeks. The maximum stock level is:

options.D: 5,000 units

e: Maximum stock level = Re-order level + Re-order quantity - (Minimum consumption x Minimum delivery period) = 2,600 + 1,800 - (200 x 3) = 3,800 units.

q: During a year, 50 workers were replaced in a factory whose average number of workers on roll was 1,250. The labour turnover rate under the replacement method is:
e: Labour turnover (replacement method) = Workers replaced / Average number of workers on roll x 100 = 50 / 1,250 x 100 = 4%.

q: Wages paid for overtime work consist of the normal wage for the overtime hours and a premium (extra payment) for those hours. In normal circumstances, the premium element of overtime wages is treated in cost accounts as:

options.A: A direct charge to the job on which the worker happened to be working
options.B: A deduction from the wages payable to the worker
options.C: Factory overheads, since the premium is not attributable to any one job
options.D: A loss charged to the Costing Profit and Loss Account

e: In normal circumstances the premium element of overtime wages is treated as factory overheads, because overtime working generally benefits production as a whole and the premium is not attributable to any one job.

q: A worker works for 54 hours in a week. The normal working week is 48 hours and the normal wage rate is Rs 40 per hour. Overtime is paid at double the normal rate. The worker's total earnings for the week are:
e: Normal wages = 48 x 40 = Rs 1,920. Overtime wages = 6 hours at double rate = 6 x 80 = Rs 480. Total earnings = 1,920 + 480 = Rs 2,400.

q: Under Gantt's task and bonus plan of wage payment:

options.A: No time wage is guaranteed; the worker is paid purely by results
options.B: The worker is guaranteed his day (time) wage, and if he completes the standard task within the standard time he receives a substantial bonus in addition to the time wage
options.C: Two piece rates are used, a lower rate below the standard and a higher rate above it, with no guaranteed wage
options.D: A bonus is paid as a fixed percentage of the time saved by the worker

e: Under Gantt's task and bonus plan, the worker is guaranteed his day (time) wage, and on completing the standard task within the standard time he receives a substantial bonus in addition to the time wage.

q: Budgeted factory overheads of a department are Rs 1,80,000 and the budgeted direct labour hours are 30,000. The direct labour hour rate for absorbing the overheads is:

options.D: Rs 60 per labour hour

e: Direct labour hour rate = Budgeted factory overheads / Budgeted direct labour hours = 1,80,000 / 30,000 = Rs 6 per labour hour.

q: A 'blanket overhead rate' means:

options.A: A rate fixed for absorbing the overheads of one department only
options.B: A rate that covers only the standing charges of a machine
options.C: A single factory-wide overhead absorption rate used for all cost centres, as distinct from separate departmental (multiple) rates for different departments
options.D: A rate revised every day on the basis of the previous day's actual overheads

e: A blanket overhead rate is a single factory-wide absorption rate used for all cost centres, as distinct from separate departmental (multiple) rates fixed for different departments.

q: Under the simultaneous equation (algebraic) method of secondary distribution of overheads:

options.A: The costs of service departments are apportioned only to production departments, the services rendered among service departments themselves being ignored
options.B: Service departments are closed one after another in a sequence and a department once closed receives no further apportionment
options.C: The apportionment is repeated again and again until the residual balances become negligible
options.D: The total cost of each service department is worked out by solving simultaneous equations, so that the services received by each service department from the others are fully recognised

e: Under the simultaneous equation method, the total cost of each service department is found by solving simultaneous equations, so the services received by each service department from the others are fully recognised.

q: The cost of idle capacity — that is, the fixed overheads relating to plant and facilities lying unused — is treated in cost accounts by:

options.A: Absorbing it in the cost of the goods actually produced, so that their unit cost rises
options.B: Excluding it from the cost of production and charging it to the Costing Profit and Loss Account
options.C: Adding it to the value of the closing stock of finished goods
options.D: Recovering it from the workers who remained idle

e: The cost of idle capacity is the fixed overhead relating to unused plant and facilities; it is excluded from the cost of production and charged to the Costing Profit and Loss Account.

q: Fixed production overheads of a factory are Rs 90,000 for a period in which production is 20,000 units and sales are 18,000 units. Compared with marginal costing, the profit under absorption costing for the period will be:

options.D: Lower by Rs 9,000

e: Fixed overhead rate = 90,000 / 20,000 units = Rs 4.50 per unit. Stock increases by 2,000 units, carrying 2,000 x 4.50 = Rs 9,000 of fixed overhead into closing stock, so absorption profit is higher by Rs 9,000.

q: In a period in which the sales exceed the production, so that the stock of finished goods decreases, the relationship between the two profits will be:

options.A: Absorption costing profit will be higher than marginal costing profit
options.B: The two profits will necessarily be equal
options.C: No profit can be computed under marginal costing in such a period
options.D: Absorption costing profit will be lower than marginal costing profit, because fixed overheads brought forward in the opening stock are released and charged against the profit of the current period

e: When sales exceed production, stock decreases and the fixed overheads brought forward in the opening stock are released and charged against the current period's profit, making absorption costing profit lower than marginal costing profit.

q: A product sells for Rs 110 per unit and its variable cost is Rs 62 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 1,92,000. The break-even point in units is:

options.D: 5,000 units

e: Break-even point = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit = 1,92,000 / (110 - 62) = 1,92,000 / 48 = 4,000 units.

q: A product sells for Rs 75 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 45 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 90,000. The number of units to be sold to earn a target profit of Rs 60,000 is:

options.D: 2,000 units

e: Units to be sold = (Fixed costs + Target profit) / Contribution per unit = (90,000 + 60,000) / (75 - 45) = 1,50,000 / 30 = 5,000 units.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 4,00,000 and its variable costs are Rs 2,60,000. Its P/V ratio is:
e: P/V ratio = (Sales - Variable costs) / Sales x 100 = (4,00,000 - 2,60,000) / 4,00,000 x 100 = 35%.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 8,00,000, its P/V ratio is 45% and its fixed costs are Rs 2,70,000. Its profit is:
Total sales of a firm are Rs 12,00,000 and its break-even sales are Rs 9,00,000. Its margin of safety as a percentage of total sales is:
e: Margin of safety = Total sales - Break-even sales = 12,00,000 - 9,00,000 = Rs 3,00,000, which is 3,00,000 / 12,00,000 x 100 = 25% of total sales.

q: The P/V ratio of a firm is 36% and its fixed costs are Rs 1,80,000. The sales required to earn a profit of Rs 90,000 are:
e: Sales required = (Fixed costs + Desired profit) / P/V ratio = (1,80,000 + 90,000) / 0.36 = 2,70,000 / 0.36 = Rs 7,50,000.

q: A factory has 15,000 machine hours available. Product A requires 5 machine hours per unit and its maximum demand is 1,800 units; production priority, on the basis of contribution per machine hour, has been given to A. Product B requires 3 machine hours per unit. After meeting the full demand for A, the number of units of B that can be produced is:

options.D: 5,000 units

e: A uses 1,800 x 5 = 9,000 machine hours for its full demand. Hours left = 15,000 - 9,000 = 6,000, giving B = 6,000 / 3 = 2,000 units.

q: Labour hours are the limiting factor in a factory. Product A gives a contribution of Rs 60 per unit and requires 4 labour hours per unit; Product B gives a contribution of Rs 77 per unit and requires 7 labour hours per unit. Production priority should be given to:

options.A: Product B, because its contribution per unit (Rs 77) is higher
options.B: Product B, because it keeps the labour engaged for more hours per unit
options.D: Product A, because its contribution per labour hour (Rs 15) is higher than that of B (Rs 11)

e: With labour hours as the limiting factor, products are ranked by contribution per labour hour: A gives 60 / 4 = Rs 15 per hour against B's 77 / 7 = Rs 11 per hour, so A gets priority.

q: A firm requires 5,000 units of a component every year. It can make the component at a variable cost of Rs 38 per unit, or buy it from an outside supplier at Rs 35 per unit. No fixed costs would be saved or incurred under either alternative, and the facilities would remain idle if the component is bought. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Make the component, because buying would save only Rs 3 per unit
options.B: Buy the component, because buying costs Rs 1,75,000 against Rs 1,90,000 for making, saving Rs 15,000 in all
options.C: Buy the component, because the saving would be Rs 3,000 in all
options.D: Remain indifferent, as the two alternatives cost the same

e: With no fixed costs saved or incurred and facilities idle if bought, only the per-unit cost matters: buying costs 5,000 x 35 = Rs 1,75,000 against making at 5,000 x 38 = Rs 1,90,000, a saving of Rs 15,000.

q: A special job requires a material which the firm already holds in stock but for which there is no other use in the factory. The material was purchased earlier at Rs 25 per kg and could now be sold as scrap for Rs 8 per kg. The relevant cost of the material for pricing the special job is:

options.A: Rs 25 per kg, being its purchase price
options.B: Nil, since the material is already in stock
options.C: Rs 8 per kg, being the amount forgone by using it on the job instead of selling it as scrap
options.D: Rs 16.50 per kg, being the average of the purchase price and the scrap value

e: The original purchase price of Rs 25 per kg is a sunk cost. The relevant cost is the opportunity cost of using the material on the job, i.e., the Rs 8 per kg scrap proceeds forgone.

q: A firm with spare capacity receives a one-time special order for 4,000 units at Rs 62 per unit. The variable cost is Rs 55 per unit, but accepting the order requires additional fixed expenditure of Rs 20,000. The order should be:

options.A: Accepted, because it yields a net incremental gain of Rs 8,000
options.B: Rejected, because the additional fixed expenditure makes it unprofitable
options.C: Accepted only if the price is raised to Rs 65 per unit
options.D: Rejected, because the price is below the firm's normal selling price

e: Incremental gain from the order = 4,000 x (62 - 55) - 20,000 additional fixed expenditure = 28,000 - 20,000 = Rs 8,000, so the special order should be accepted.

q: A firm with spare capacity is negotiating a one-time special order. The minimum price at which the order can be accepted without loss is the price which covers:

options.A: The full absorption cost of the order, including a share of the existing fixed overheads
options.B: The normal selling price charged to regular customers
options.C: The prime cost of the order only
options.D: The incremental costs of executing the order, that is, its variable cost plus any additional fixed costs specially incurred for the order

e: With spare capacity, existing fixed overheads are incurred anyway, so only the extra costs caused by the order matter: the minimum acceptable price covers its variable cost plus any extra fixed costs specially incurred for it.

q: The total fixed costs of a plant are Rs 5,00,000 per year, of which Rs 2,00,000 would continue to be incurred even during a shutdown; in addition, discontinuance (shutdown) costs of Rs 50,000 would be incurred if the plant is closed. The contribution is Rs 35 per unit. The shutdown point is:

options.D: 7,143 units

e: Shutdown point = (total fixed costs - unavoidable fixed costs + shutdown costs) / contribution = (5,00,000 - 2,00,000 + 50,000) / 35 = 3,50,000 / 35 = 10,000 units.

q: A division earns a contribution of Rs 60,000. Its avoidable (specific) fixed costs are Rs 75,000, besides which Rs 40,000 of common fixed costs are allocated to it and would continue even if the division were closed. If the division is closed down, the total profit of the company will:

options.D: Decrease by Rs 55,000

e: Closing removes the contribution of Rs 60,000 but saves the avoidable fixed costs of Rs 75,000; the common Rs 40,000 continues anyway. Net effect = 75,000 - 60,000 = Rs 15,000 increase in profit.

q: For the actual output, the standard quantity of material is 2,000 kg at a standard price of Rs 8 per kg. The actual quantity consumed is 2,200 kg purchased at Rs 9 per kg. The material cost variance is:

options.D: Rs 3,800 (Adverse)

e: Material cost variance = (standard quantity x standard price) - (actual quantity x actual price) = (2,000 x 8) - (2,200 x 9) = 16,000 - 19,800 = Rs 3,800 (Adverse).

q: For the actual output, the standard labour time is 800 hours, but only 750 hours were actually taken. The standard wage rate is Rs 40 per hour. The labour efficiency variance is:

options.D: Rs 1,500 (Favourable)

e: Labour efficiency variance = (standard hours - actual hours) x standard rate = (800 - 750) x 40 = 50 x 40 = Rs 2,000 (Favourable), since fewer hours were taken than standard.

q: The budgeted fixed overheads of a factory for a period are Rs 1,20,000 and the actual fixed overheads incurred are Rs 1,35,000. The fixed overhead expenditure variance is:

options.D: Nil

e: Fixed overhead expenditure variance = budgeted fixed overheads - actual fixed overheads = 1,20,000 - 1,35,000 = Rs 15,000 (Adverse), because actual spending exceeded the budget.

q: The budgeted production of a factory is 25,000 units and the standard fixed overhead rate is Rs 3 per unit. Actual production is 22,000 units. The fixed overhead volume variance is:

options.D: Rs 66,000 (Adverse)

e: Volume variance = (actual output - budgeted output) x standard rate per unit = (22,000 - 25,000) x 3 = Rs 9,000 (Adverse), as production fell short of budget.

q: The labour gang (mix) variance arises when:

options.A: The actual wage rate paid differs from the standard wage rate
options.B: The actual hours worked exceed the standard hours for the output
options.C: Some hours are lost as idle time during production
options.D: The actual composition of the labour gang (the proportion of skilled, semi-skilled and unskilled workers) differs from the standard gang composition

e: The gang or mix variance arises because the actual proportion of skilled, semi-skilled and unskilled workers in the gang differs from the standard gang composition, even if total hours agree with standard.

q: In a process, 2,000 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 46,000. Normal loss is 10% of the input and the scrap realises Rs 5 per unit. The cost per unit of good output is:
e: Cost per unit = (total cost - scrap value of normal loss) / expected good output = (46,000 - 200 x 5) / (2,000 - 200) = 45,000 / 1,800 = Rs 25.00.

q: In a process, 1,500 units are introduced and the normal loss is 10% of the input. The actual output obtained is 1,275 units. The abnormal loss is:

options.D: Nil

e: Expected output = 1,500 - 10% normal loss = 1,350 units. Actual output is 1,275 units, so abnormal loss = 1,350 - 1,275 = 75 units.

q: In a process, 4,000 units were completed and transferred to the next process during a period. The closing work-in-progress is 1,000 units, which are 50% complete in respect of all cost elements, and there was no opening work-in-progress. The equivalent production for the period is:

options.D: 4,250 units

e: Equivalent production = completed units + closing WIP at its degree of completion = 4,000 + (1,000 x 50%) = 4,000 + 500 = 4,500 units.

q: A transport undertaking incurs a total operating cost of Rs 12,00,000 during a period in which its vehicles run 3,00,000 kilometres. The operating cost per vehicle-kilometre is:
e: Operating cost per vehicle-km = total operating cost / total kilometres run = 12,00,000 / 3,00,000 = Rs 4.00 per vehicle-kilometre.

q: Operating (service) costing commonly uses composite cost units, that is:

options.A: A combination of two measures, such as cost per passenger-kilometre for a transport undertaking, cost per patient-day for a hospital or cost per room-day for a hotel
options.B: The cost of manufacturing one unit of the finished product
options.C: The cost per machine hour of running a machine
options.D: The cost expressed as a percentage of the sales value

e: Operating costing uses composite units combining two measures of service, such as passenger-kilometre, patient-day or room-day, because the service rendered has both a quantity and a distance or time dimension.

q: Under activity-based costing, the power cost pool of a plant is Rs 2,70,000 and the total machine hours worked in the period are 9,000. A product which uses 1,600 machine hours will be assigned power cost of:
e: Power cost rate = 2,70,000 / 9,000 machine hours = Rs 30 per machine hour. Cost assigned = 1,600 x 30 = Rs 48,000.

q: A recognised weakness of traditional costing, which activity-based costing seeks to remove, is that:

options.A: It charges too much overhead to all products without exception
options.B: Allocating overheads on a volume basis such as labour hours tends to over-cost high-volume, simple products and under-cost low-volume, complex products, because overheads are driven by the diversity and complexity of activities and not by volume alone
options.C: It ignores the direct costs of products altogether
options.D: It can be applied only to service undertakings and not to factories

e: Volume-based allocation assumes overheads vary with output volume, but they are actually driven by activities and complexity; so simple high-volume products absorb too much overhead and complex low-volume products too little.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 3,00,000 and is expected to yield net cash inflows of Rs 1,20,000 at the end of Year 1 (present value factor at 10% = 0.909) and Rs 1,50,000 at the end of Year 2 (present value factor at 10% = 0.826). The Net Present Value of the project is:

A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 6,00,000 and is expected to yield a net cash inflow of Rs 2,00,000 at the end of each of the next 4 years. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 4 years at 10% is 3.170. The Net Present Value of the project is:
e: NPV = (2,00,000 x 3.170) - 6,00,000 = 6,34,000 - 6,00,000 = (+) Rs 34,000; a positive NPV means the project earns more than the 10% cost of capital.

q: A machine costing Rs 9,00,000 generates a net cash inflow of Rs 1,80,000 per year. Its payback period is:

options.D: 5.5 years

e: Payback period = initial cost / annual cash inflow = 9,00,000 / 1,80,000 = 5 years, the time taken for inflows to recover the outlay.

q: A project costing Rs 4,00,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 80,000 in Year 1, Rs 1,20,000 in Year 2, Rs 1,60,000 in Year 3 and Rs 80,000 in Year 4. Its payback period is:

options.D: 3 years 6 months

e: Cumulative inflows: 80,000, 2,00,000, 3,60,000, 4,40,000. The Rs 4,00,000 outlay is recovered in Year 4: 3 years + (40,000 / 80,000) = 3 years 6 months.

q: A project involves an initial outlay of Rs 3,00,000. The discounted (present) values of its cash inflows are Rs 80,000 at the end of Year 1, Rs 1,00,000 at the end of Year 2, Rs 1,00,000 at the end of Year 3 and Rs 60,000 at the end of Year 4. The discounted payback period of the project is:

options.D: 2 years 10 months

e: Cumulative present values: 80,000, 1,80,000, 2,80,000, 3,40,000. The Rs 3,00,000 outlay is recovered in Year 4: 3 years + (20,000 / 60,000) of a year = 3 years 4 months.

q: A project's NPV is (+) Rs 6,000 at a discount rate of 12% and (-) Rs 4,000 at a discount rate of 15%. By interpolation, its internal rate of return is approximately:
e: IRR = 12% + [6,000 / (6,000 + 4,000)] x (15 - 12)% = 12% + 0.6 x 3% = 13.8%, by interpolation between the positive and negative NPV rates.

q: The present value of the future cash inflows of a project is Rs 5,50,000 and its initial investment is Rs 5,00,000. The Profitability Index of the project is:
e: Profitability Index = present value of inflows / initial investment = 5,50,000 / 5,00,000 = 1.10; a PI above 1 indicates a positive NPV.

q: An investment of Rs 6,00,000 has an expected salvage value of Rs 1,00,000 at the end of its life, so that the average investment is Rs 3,50,000. If the average annual profit after depreciation and tax is Rs 52,500, the Average Rate of Return computed on the average investment is:
Under the Net Present Value method, the intermediate cash inflows of a project are implicitly assumed to be reinvested at:

options.A: The internal rate of return of the project
options.B: The cost of capital of the enterprise
options.D: The rate of inflation

e: NPV discounts all cash flows at the cost of capital, so it implicitly assumes intermediate inflows are reinvested at that same rate, the cost of capital.

q: Two projects are said to be mutually exclusive when:

options.A: Both of them can be accepted and executed together
options.B: Neither of them depends on the other in any way
options.C: The acceptance of one of them automatically excludes the acceptance of the other
options.D: Both of them have the same initial cost

e: Mutually exclusive projects compete for the same purpose, so choosing one automatically rejects the other, unlike independent projects which can all be accepted if worthwhile.

q: When an existing machine is replaced by a new machine, the salvage (realisable) value of the old machine is treated in the capital budgeting analysis as:

options.A: A cash inflow at the time of replacement, reducing the net cash outlay on the new machine
options.B: Ignored altogether, since the old machine is fully depreciated
options.C: An income to be spread evenly over the life of the new machine
options.D: An addition to the cost of the new machine

e: The salvage value of the old machine is a cash inflow at the replacement date; it reduces the net investment required for the new machine in the analysis.

q: A post-completion audit (post-audit) of a capital project means:

options.A: The statutory audit of the project accounts by the C&AG before the project is sanctioned
options.B: A technical feasibility study carried out before the project is taken up
options.C: A re-estimation of the project cost midway through its execution
options.D: A comparison, after completion, of the actual costs and benefits of the project with the original estimates, so that future appraisals can be improved

e: A post-completion audit compares actual project costs and benefits with the original estimates after completion, feeding lessons back to improve future capital expenditure appraisals.

q: A company's capital structure consists of equity capital of Rs 5,00,000 (cost 16%), preference capital of Rs 3,00,000 (cost 12%) and debt of Rs 2,00,000 (after-tax cost 6%). Its weighted average cost of capital is:
e: WACC = (5/10 x 16%) + (3/10 x 12%) + (2/10 x 6%) = 8% + 3.6% + 1.2% = 12.8%, weighting each source by its share of capital.

q: A company issues 12% debentures of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 96 per debenture. Ignoring tax and redemption premium, the cost of debt is:
e: Ignoring tax, cost of debt = annual interest / issue proceeds = 12 / 96 = 12.5%; issuing at a discount raises the effective cost above the coupon rate.

q: A share is expected to pay a constant dividend of Rs 9 per share every year and its market price is Rs 75 per share. The cost of equity capital is:
e: For a constant (zero-growth) dividend, cost of equity = dividend / market price = 9 / 75 = 12%.

q: A share is expected to pay a dividend of Rs 5 per share next year. Its market price is Rs 40 and dividends are expected to grow at a constant rate of 3% per year. Using the dividend growth model, the cost of equity is:
e: Dividend growth model: cost of equity = (expected dividend / price) + growth = (5 / 40) + 3% = 12.5% + 3% = 15.5%.

q: Using the Capital Asset Pricing Model, where the risk-free rate is 6%, the expected market return is 14% and the beta of the share is 0.8, the cost of equity is:
e: CAPM: cost of equity = risk-free rate + beta x (market return - risk-free rate) = 6% + 0.8 x (14% - 6%) = 6% + 6.4% = 12.4%.

q: In the Capital Asset Pricing Model, the 'beta' of a share measures its:

options.B: Total risk, both systematic and unsystematic
options.D: Liquidity risk

e: Beta measures systematic, market-wide risk that cannot be diversified away; it shows how a share's return moves with the market as a whole.

q: Under the Net Operating Income (NOI) approach to capital structure:

options.A: The overall cost of capital falls continuously as more and more debt is used
options.B: The overall (weighted average) cost of capital remains constant at all levels of leverage, because the benefit of cheaper debt is exactly offset by the rise in the cost of equity
options.C: The value of the firm falls as debt increases
options.D: The cost of equity remains constant at all levels of leverage

e: Under the NOI approach the total value and overall cost of capital are independent of leverage: cheaper debt is exactly offset by a rising cost of equity, keeping WACC constant.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 25,00,000, variable costs are Rs 15,00,000 and fixed costs are Rs 6,00,000. The degree of operating leverage is:
An enterprise has earnings before interest and tax of Rs 5,00,000 and pays interest of Rs 1,00,000. Its degree of financial leverage is:
e: Degree of financial leverage = EBIT / (EBIT - interest) = 5,00,000 / (5,00,000 - 1,00,000) = 5,00,000 / 4,00,000 = 1.25.

q: An enterprise has sales of Rs 20,00,000, variable costs of Rs 10,00,000, fixed costs of Rs 4,00,000 and interest of Rs 2,00,000. Its degree of combined leverage is:
e: Degree of combined leverage = contribution / (EBIT - interest) = 10,00,000 / (6,00,000 - 2,00,000) = 10,00,000 / 4,00,000 = 2.5; it combines operating and financial leverage.

q: If an enterprise has no fixed operating costs at all, its degree of operating leverage will be:

options.D: One (unity)

e: With no fixed operating costs, contribution equals EBIT, so DOL = contribution / EBIT = 1; a given percentage change in sales produces an equal change in EBIT.

q: The degree of financial leverage primarily measures:

options.A: The sensitivity of the earnings available to equity shareholders (EPS) to changes in the earnings before interest and tax (EBIT)
options.B: The sensitivity of sales to changes in the selling price
options.C: The sensitivity of EBIT to changes in sales
options.D: The sensitivity of interest charges to changes in the amount of debt

e: Financial leverage arises from fixed interest charges, so DFL measures how sensitive EPS is to a change in EBIT: a given EBIT change produces a magnified EPS change.

q: Under the traditional approach to capital structure:

options.A: The weighted average cost of capital rises from the very first use of debt
options.B: The weighted average cost of capital is unaffected by the proportion of debt
options.C: A judicious use of debt first lowers the weighted average cost of capital, but beyond an optimum point further debt raises it, so that an optimum capital structure exists
options.D: The maximum possible debt is always the best capital structure

e: The traditional approach holds that moderate debt lowers WACC because debt is cheaper, but beyond the optimum level the rising costs of equity and debt push WACC up again.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 9,00,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 6,00,000. Its current ratio is:
e: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities = 9,00,000 / 6,00,000 = 1.5 : 1.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 6,00,000, comprising stock of Rs 2,50,000 and prepaid expenses of Rs 50,000. Current liabilities are Rs 2,00,000. The quick (acid-test) ratio is:
e: Quick assets exclude stock and prepaid expenses: 6,00,000 - 2,50,000 - 50,000 = 3,00,000. Quick ratio = 3,00,000 / 2,00,000 = 1.5 : 1.

q: Proprietors' funds of an enterprise are Rs 9,00,000 and its total assets are Rs 12,00,000. The proprietary ratio is:
e: Proprietary ratio = proprietors' funds / total assets = 9,00,000 / 12,00,000 = 0.75 : 1, showing 75% of assets are financed by owners' funds.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 12,00,000 and the cost of goods sold is Rs 9,00,000. Its gross profit ratio is:
The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 1,50,000 on sales of Rs 15,00,000. Its net profit ratio is:
e: Net profit ratio = net profit / sales x 100 = 1,50,000 / 15,00,000 x 100 = 10%.

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise is Rs 14,00,000 and its average inventory is Rs 2,00,000. The inventory turnover ratio is:

options.D: 7 times

e: Inventory turnover = cost of goods sold / average inventory = 14,00,000 / 2,00,000 = 7 times.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 7,50,000 and its average debtors are Rs 1,50,000. The debtors turnover ratio is:

options.D: 0.2 times

e: Debtors turnover = credit sales / average debtors = 7,50,000 / 1,50,000 = 5 times.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 14,60,000 and its average debtors are Rs 1,60,000. Taking a year of 365 days, the average collection period is:

options.D: 50 days

e: Average collection period = (average debtors / credit sales) x 365 = (1,60,000 / 14,60,000) x 365 = 40 days.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 10,00,000 and the interest payable is Rs 4,00,000. The interest coverage ratio is:

options.D: 0.4 times

e: Interest coverage = profit before interest and tax / interest = 10,00,000 / 4,00,000 = 2.5 times, showing the margin of safety for lenders.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 4,50,000 and its capital employed is Rs 15,00,000. The Return on Capital Employed is:
e: Return on Capital Employed = (4,50,000 / 15,00,000) x 100 = 30%.
